{"filepath":"research_findings.md","content":"# Air‑Source Heat Pumps (ASHP) — UK-focused research findings

Date: 06 September 2026
Prepared by: Research Specialist (AI)

Contents
- Executive summary
- How air‑source heat pumps work
- Typical benefits and limitations
- Performance metrics (COP, SCOP) and typical seasonal performance for UK climate
- Sizing and installation considerations
- Typical purchase and installation costs and ranges (UK)
- Typical running costs and example savings vs gas/oil
- Noise and space requirements
- Maintenance needs and expected lifetime
- UK policy and grant support (overview)
- Common homeowner FAQs & misconceptions
- Practical next steps for homeowner-facing explainer and recommended primary sources to collect
- References and links


Executive summary
-----------------
Air‑source heat pumps (ASHPs) extract energy from outside air and use a refrigeration cycle to raise its temperature so it can heat a home and supply hot water. In the UK they are the most common domestic heat pump type because they are relatively small and cheaper to install than ground‑source heat pumps.

Key UK points summarized:
- Typical seasonal performance (SCOP) for modern ASHPs in UK conditions commonly falls in the ~2.8–3.8 range, giving several units of heat per unit of electricity used (eg. COP at a particular outdoor temperature typically 2.5–4.5).
- Upfront installation costs are higher than a like‑for‑like gas boiler replacement; typical installed costs in the UK are commonly reported in the ~£6,000–£15,000 range depending on home, system size and complexity. Public grants (Boiler Upgrade Scheme) have reduced homeowner net cost by up to ~£7,500 for eligible installs in England & Wales.
- Running costs vs gas/oil depend strongly on system efficiency (real SCOP), building fabric (insulation, low distribution temperatures), and electricity tariff (standard vs time‑of‑use / heat‑pump tariff). On typical assumptions a well‑sized ASHP in a well‑insulated home on a heat‑pump tariff will usually reduce carbon emissions and often reduce fuel bills versus electric heating; savings vs modern gas boilers vary and can be modest or negative depending on prices and performance. 

(See full sections below for details, tables and recommended citation links.)


How air‑source heat pumps work
--------------------------------
- Core concept: ASHPs move heat from outdoor air into the heating system using a vapor‑compression refrigeration cycle (evaporator, compressor, condenser, expansion valve).
- The outdoor unit contains the evaporator and fan which extracts low‑grade heat from ambient air. A refrigerant evaporates at a low temperature, is compressed (raising its temperature), and the hot refrigerant condenses in a heat exchanger to transfer heat to water (air‑to‑water ASHP) or to air (air‑to‑air ASHP).
- Most UK domestic ASHPs are air‑to‑water and are used with underfloor heating or with radiators sized for lower flow temperatures (e.g., 35–55°C) and with a hot water cylinder for domestic hot water.
- ASHPs can operate in reverse to provide cooling in some configurations.

Primary explanatory references (UK):
- Energy Saving Trust — in‑depth guide to heat pumps (UK): https://energysavingtrust.org.uk/advice/in-depth-guide-to-heat-pumps
- GOV.UK Q&A: Heat pumps explained (experts answer your questions): https://www.gov.uk/government/news/heat-pumps-explained-experts-answer-your-questions
- National Grid: How does an air‑source heat pump work? https://www.nationalgrid.com/stories/energy-explained/how-do-heat-pumps-work


Typical benefits and limitations
---------------------------------
Benefits
- High efficiency: ASHPs typically deliver multiple kWh of heat per kWh of electricity (COP >1), reducing primary energy use compared to direct electric resistance heating.
- Lower operational carbon when grid electricity is low‑carbon (and particularly if paired with low‑carbon tariffs or onsite renewables).
- No on‑site combustion: safer (no flue), can be installed where gas is not available.
- Can provide both space heating and hot water; some models provide limited cooling.
- Eligible for government grants (see policy section).

Limitations and constraints
- Upfront cost: higher capital cost than replacing a gas boiler, though grants reduce net cost for eligible households.
- Performance falls with colder outdoor temperatures — instantaneous COP is lower during cold snaps; seasonal performance (SCOP) is the more relevant metric.
- Requires low‑temperature distribution (large radiators or underfloor heating) for best efficiency and comfort in many UK homes. Older homes with small radiators or poor fabric may need additional upgrades (insulation, radiator sizing) to get best results.
- Noise and siting: outdoor units have fans and compressors and require careful siting to manage noise and neighbours' concerns.
- Space for outdoor unit and often for a hot‑water cylinder inside; planning and property constraints can affect feasibility.


Performance metrics (COP, SCOP) and typical seasonal performance for UK climate
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Definitions
- COP (Coefficient of Performance): instantaneous ratio of heat power output to electrical power input at a given set of conditions (e.g., outdoor temp = 7°C, flow temperature = 35°C).
- SCOP (Seasonal COP): weighted average COP across a typical heating season; it accounts for varying outdoor temperatures and realistic operation and is the best single figure for estimating annual performance and running costs.

Typical ranges (UK context — indicative):
| Metric | Typical range (modern domestic ASHP) | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| Instantaneous COP (moderate conditions) | 2.5 – 4.5 | Varies with outdoor temp and flow temp; measured at e.g. 7°C reference point for some standards. |
| SCOP (seasonal, UK) | 2.8 – 3.8 (common) | Many compliant installations fall in this range; higher for well‑matched systems and low distribution temperatures. |
| Minimum MCS allowed SCOP for compliant installations | ~2.8 | Industry guidance often references minimum thresholds for certification/schemes. |

Notes on seasonal/real‑world behaviour
- COP falls as outdoor temperature drops and/or as required flow temperature rises (e.g., when heating demand is high). Thus winter cold snaps reduce instantaneous COP and increase electricity consumption per kWh of heat delivered.
- Real household SCOP depends on heat pump sizing, building heat demand profile, hot water load, system controls, and installer quality.

Sources used for performance ranges (examples):
- Industry and installation guides summarise SCOP/COP concepts and typical ranges; see Energy Saving Trust guide and industry explainers. (See references.)


Sizing and installation considerations
-------------------------------------
Overview of key considerations
- Heat demand calculation: a proper room‑by‑room heat loss calculation (or an accredited domestic SAP / RdSAP / SAP‑based or Dynamic Thermal Modelling where relevant) should determine required heating capacity; avoid oversizing which can reduce seasonal efficiency and increase costs.
- Flow temperature targets: design the system for low distribution temperatures (ideally 35–45°C for best SCOP where possible) — this may require larger radiators or underfloor heating to meet heat demand comfortably.
- Buffer/hot‑water cylinder: an ASHP typically requires or benefits from a thermal store (hot water cylinder) sized appropriately to household hot water demand; some units integrate or are paired with cylinders.
- Siting: outdoor unit needs unobstructed airflow and sufficient clearance; choose a location to minimise noise impact on neighbours and to ease service access. Local planning and building control advice should be checked for listed/building‑conservation areas.
- Electrical supply: check mains capacity and whether any electrical upgrade is needed (some larger ASHPs or hybrid systems may require a three‑phase or increased single‑phase supply). Metering and tariff choices (time‑of‑use) should be considered.
- Controls and zoning: modern controls (smart thermostats, weather compensation, hot water scheduling) improve performance and comfort. Zoning reduces waste heating of unused rooms.
- Installer accreditation: use MCS‑certified or otherwise accredited installers (or manufacturer‑recommended) to ensure correct sizing, commissioning and eligibility for some grants.

Installation steps (typical)
1. Survey and heat loss/heat demand calculation
2. System design (radiator/upgrading distribution, cylinder sizing, controls)
3. Selecting ASHP model and location of outdoor/indoor units
4. Installation of outdoor unit, internal hydraulic work, cylinder and controls
5. Commissioning, performance tests and user briefing
6. Registering warranties and any grant applications (installer often handles BUS application if eligible)


Typical purchase and installation costs and ranges (UK)
------------------------------------------------------
Notes on prices
- Reported prices vary widely with property size, system complexity, region and installer. Public grants (Boiler Upgrade Scheme — BUS) reduce net cost for many homeowners.
- The market has evolved; sources sampled during this research reported overlapping but not identical ranges. Use the ranges below as indicative (2024–2026 market context):

Indicative installed cost ranges (ASHP, UK, pre/post‑grant)
| Item | Typical range (GBP) |
|---|---:|
| Heat pump unit (domestic ASHP) | £3,000 – £8,000 (depending on capacity and make) |
| Typical full supply & install (small/medium house) | £6,000 – £15,000 |
| Typical full supply & install (larger or complex installations) | £12,000 – £20,000+ |
| Typical net cost after Boiler Upgrade Scheme (BUS) grant (England & Wales, where eligible) | ~£(cost above) − £7,500 (grant) |

Representative figures reported by industry sources sampled:
- Some installers and guides report typical installed costs around £8,000–£11,000; others show broader ranges £6,000–£15,000 depending on scope.

Important caveats
- These are market‑level indicative numbers. Obtain at least 3 written quotes from MCS‑certified installers for a specific property. Quotes should include: detailed equipment spec, expected seasonal performance (SCOP), radiator/upgrading requirements and commissioning measures, and warranty terms.


Typical running costs and example savings vs gas/oil
----------------------------------------------------
How to estimate running cost
- Annual running cost ≈ (annual heat demand ÷ SCOP) × electricity unit price + standing charges + hot‑water reheating overheads + any supplementary electric boost usage.
- Compare with gas/oil by converting annual heat demand ÷ boiler efficiency × fuel unit price.

Indicative example (illustrative only)
- Assumptions: detached/medium UK house annual heat demand ~12,000 kWh (space heating + hot water simplified), ASHP seasonal COP (SCOP) = 3.0, electricity price = £0.30/kWh (example retail price), gas boiler efficiency = 90%, gas price = £0.07/kWh (example delivered price). 

Running cost ASHP: (12,000 kWh ÷ 3.0) × £0.30 = 4,000 kWh_elec × £0.30 = £1,200
Running cost gas boiler: (12,000 kWh ÷ 0.90) × £0.07 = 13,333 kWh_gas × £0.07 = £933

- In this illustrative scenario the ASHP costs more to run (£1,200 vs £933) because (a) electricity price per kWh is higher than gas, and (b) SCOP is only 3.0. If electricity price falls (or a heat‑pump tariff is used) or SCOP rises (e.g., 3.5–4.0) the ASHP becomes cheaper to run.

Sensitivity and real‑world notes
- The running cost comparison is highly sensitive to: actual SCOP, the electricity tariff (standard vs time‑of‑use or bespoke heat‑pump tariffs), how well the home is insulated (heat demand), and the gas price. With current/future grid decarbonisation and targeted tariffs, many homeowners can achieve running cost parity or savings.
- Energy Saving Trust and other organisations note that a well‑installed ASHP on a suitable tariff in a well‑insulated home often saves money vs electric resistance heating and reduces carbon vs gas; savings vs modern gas boilers can be modest unless electricity is cheap or SCOP is high.

Sources & discussion: see Energy Saving Trust guide and industry comparison pages (references).


Noise and space requirements
----------------------------
Typical considerations
- Outdoor units contain fans and compressors. Noise is typically quoted by manufacturers as sound power level (LwA) or sound pressure level at a given distance (Lp at 1 m or 3 m). Typical modern domestic ASHP noise quoted by manufacturers often sits in the mid‑40s to mid‑50s dB(A) range at 1 m on higher fan speeds (models and modes vary). Low‑noise models and low‑noise operating modes are available that reduce perceived impact.
- Careful siting (mounting on vibration‑reducing pads, choosing locations away from neighbours’ windows, installing acoustic screens where necessary) greatly reduces the likelihood of complaints.
- Outdoor unit footprint is typically similar to two wheelie bins side‑by‑side (typical monoblock ASHP), but dimensions depend on model. Indoor space for a hot water cylinder or buffer vessel must be provided.
- Local authority nuisance/noise guidance should be checked for installations near boundaries; some local planning constraints may apply for listed buildings or conservation areas.

Note: model‑specific datasheets give exact dimensions and manufacturer noise figures — consult datasheets when specifying and request predicted noise contours from installers.


Maintenance needs and expected lifetime
----------------------------------------
Maintenance
- Annual or biennial service recommended: check fans, refrigerant charge (technician checks), hydraulic circuits, controls, and electrical connections.
- Homeowner tasks: keep external unit clear of leaves/debris, keep intake/exhaust free, ensure cylinder drainage and condensate are functioning, check frost/defrost operation in winter and report unusual noises.
- Manufacturer recommended service intervals vary; warranty conditions often require regular servicing by accredited engineers to remain valid.

Lifetime
- Typical design life: 15–20 years for domestic ASHPs; some systems last longer with good maintenance. Many manufacturers provide 5‑10 year warranties on compressors/parts (extended warranties available).

Replacement components
- Compressors or major components can be expensive to replace; consider service contracts or extended warranties if concerned about mid‑life costs.


UK policy and grant support (overview)
--------------------------------------
Boiler Upgrade Scheme (BUS)
- The Government introduced the Boiler Upgrade Scheme to support replacement of fossil‑fuel boilers with low‑carbon heating (heat pumps and biomass where applicable). Typical reported grant value for domestic ASHPs is up to £7,500 for eligible household installs in England & Wales (scheme launched 2022; check current eligibility, application process and available budgets). Installers typically apply for the BUS grant on behalf of eligible customers.

Other UK support and local schemes
- Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland may have different or additional schemes and incentives (e.g., Home Energy Scotland, local authority grants or financing). Some devolved programmes can have higher or complementary support. Check local government portals and manufacturer offers.

Regulatory and industry schemes
- MCS (Microgeneration Certification Scheme) standards and installer accreditation are commonly required for certain grants and provide assurance regarding installation standards.

Note and action: confirm up‑to‑date BUS rules, eligibility and amounts on gov.uk and contact local energy advice services for devolved/national schemes and any new incentives introduced since this report.


Common homeowner FAQs and misconceptions
----------------------------------------
Q: Will a heat pump work in cold UK winters?
A: Yes — modern ASHPs operate in UK winter temperatures and are widely used across the country. Performance (instantaneous COP) reduces in very cold weather, but seasonal performance (SCOP) captures realistic winter behaviour. Homes with high heat demands or poor insulation may need distribution upgrades (bigger radiators or underfloor heating) for comfort.

Q: Are heat pumps noisy?
A: Outdoor units produce fan/compressor noise. Modern units are designed to be relatively quiet; typical outdoor sound pressure levels quoted by manufacturers often fall in the mid‑40s to mid‑50s dB(A) depending on fan speed and model. Correct siting and low‑noise models mitigate impact.

Q: Do I need new radiators or underfloor heating?
A: Often an ASHP performs best with lower flow temperatures. Many installations keep existing radiators if they are sufficiently sized; smaller radiators or very old systems may need upsizing or underfloor heating for efficient, comfortable operation.

Q: Will I save money vs a gas boiler?
A: It depends. Savings depend on SCOP, electricity and gas prices, insulation and controls. In many cases ASHPs reduce carbon and can be cost‑effective on specialist tariffs or where grants reduce upfront costs. For some homes, particularly poorly insulated ones or where electricity is expensive and SCOP is low, gas may remain cheaper to run.

Q: How often does it need servicing?
A: Annual or biennial technical service is recommended; basic external cleaning/clearance is a homeowner task.

Q: Can I still get grants?
A: England & Wales: Boiler Upgrade Scheme has provided grants (commonly reported up to £7,500 for ASHPs). Check current eligibility and application routes on gov.uk and through your installer.

Q: Are heat pumps suitable for listed or conservation properties?
A: Possibly, but external unit siting, visual impact and planning constraints must be discussed with local planning authorities. Hybrid or alternative measures may be considered where full replacement is restricted.


Practical next steps (for the writer and for homeowners)
--------------------------------------------------------
- Collect up‑to‑date manufacturer datasheets for 3–5 mainstream models (e.g., Daikin Altherma, Mitsubishi Ecodan, NIBE, Samsung EHS) and include specific COP/SCOP, noise (dB) and physical dimensions for homeowner comparison.
- Obtain independent test reports (e.g., Which? reviews if available, BRE testing, or accredited lab tests) for real‑world performance comparisons.
- Confirm current Boiler Upgrade Scheme (BUS) rules and any devolved nation variations (Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland) via gov.uk and relevant devolved government web pages.
- Ask 3 accredited (MCS) installers for quotes for a range of typical UK property archetypes (medium semi, detached, small flat) and request full breakdowns (equipment, radiator upgrade costs, cylinder, commissioning, warranties).


Recommended primary sources to collect (high priority)
- GOV.UK Boiler Upgrade Scheme page and guidance (official BUS page)
- Energy Saving Trust — heat pumps in‑depth guide (already referenced)
- MCS / BEIS technical certification pages for heat pumps
- Manufacturer product datasheets (Daikin, Mitsubishi Electric, NIBE, Vaillant, Worcester/Bosch, Samsung etc.) for commonly installed models in the UK
- Independent test/review sources: Which? product tests, trusted industry test reports, National Physical Laboratory or BRE if available
- Local authority planning/noise guidance and Building Regulations guidance (Part L) references where relevant


References and links (sources used during this search)
- Energy Saving Trust — in‑depth guide to heat pumps: https://energysavingtrust.org.uk/advice/in-depth-guide-to-heat-pumps
- GOV.UK — Heat pumps explained: experts answer your questions: https://www.gov.uk/government/news/heat-pumps-explained-experts-answer-your-questions
- National Grid — How does an air‑source heat pump work?: https://www.nationalgrid.com/stories/energy-explained/how-do-heat-pumps-work
- Wikipedia — Air source heat pump (process and general description): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_source_heat_pump
- Representative cost pages and industry guides sampled during research:
  - uandirenewables.co.uk — Air Source Heat Pump Costs UK (example industry guide)
  - whatprice.co.uk — Air Source Heat Pump Cost (market price guide)
  - myjobquote.co.uk — Installation cost guide
  (Note: these are commercial guides; obtain installer quotes for site‑specific pricing.)


Limitations of this file and notes for reviewer
----------------------------------------------
- Web search quota exhausted during research. The core government and industry guidance links above were captured and included, but the file does not include direct manufacturer datasheet links or independent test reports (Which?, BRE tests, etc.) — the next step should fetch and cite these primary documents.
- Cost and running‑cost examples are indicative and sensitive to prices and tariff assumptions; they should be converted into a small table of worked examples in the homeowner explainer using up‑to‑date unit prices before publication.


End of research_findings.md
